A 27-year-old Japanese man presented with a 2-day history of posterior neck pain, sore throat, and odynophagia. He had no history of trauma, upper respiratory infection, or dental problems. On examination, active cervical range of motion was severely reduced by pain localized to the posterior neck. Oropharyngeal examination was normal, and there were no neurologic deficits. His temperature was 37.5°C. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 12,500/mm³ and a C-reactive protein level of 1.0 mg/dL. A lateral cervical-spine radiograph revealed retropharyngeal thickening at the upper cervical spine and soft-tissue calcification anterior to the C1 arch. Unenhanced CT of the cervical spine demonstrated soft-tissue calcification extending from the longus colli muscle to the atlanto-odontoid joint.

A woman in her mid-60s presented to the emergency department with sudden, dull left flank pain, rated 8 of 10, radiating to the lateral abdomen and accompanied by nausea. No exacerbating or alleviating factors were noted. She was a nonsmoker and did not report recreational drugs or alcohol. Family history notable for father with renal cell carcinoma. Medical history included hypertension, basal cell carcinoma in remission, and an autoimmune condition diagnosed 16 years ago. Patient had been on long-term azathioprine therapy (125 mg daily, later reduced to 100 mg daily) and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. Four years after initial diagnosis, she experienced unintentional weight loss, fever, polyarthralgia, and fatigue.

Patient was hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed tenderness at the left costovertebral angle.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Hemoglobin: 114 g/L (Normal: 125-165)    * WBC: 6.17 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 4-10.8)    * ANC: 2.75 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 1.5-7.8)    * ALC: 3.32 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 0.85-3.9)    * AMC: 1.15 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 0.299-0.95)    * AEC: 0.12 ×10⁹/L (Normal: 0.02-0.5)    * LDH: 3.03 µkat/L (Normal: 2.33-4.67)    * Creatinine: 95.47 µmol/L (Normal: 53.04-97.24)    * ESR: 54 mm/hr (Normal: 0-20)    * CRP: 6.1 mg/L (Normal: <8)  - Imaging Studies:    * CT Scan Title: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen    * CT Scan Description: 7 cm × 5 cm × 5 cm heterogenous left adrenal mass containing regions of necrosis, with local extension into and invasion of the pancreatic tail, left hemidiaphragm, and spleen, along with the presence of multiple enlarged regional lymph nodes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Epstein-Barr virus–associated polymorphic lymphoproliferative disorder involving the adrenal gland

clinical_record:
An 8-year-old girl weighing 44.5 kg with no significant medical history presented with a 1-week history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination revealed notable abdominal distension without guarding or rebound. Initial abdominal ultrasonography showed a 17 × 9 cm mixed solid and cystic mass occupying the right hepatic lobe with compression of the inferior vena cava (IVC). By hospital day 7, worsening abdominal distension and concern for abdominal compartment syndrome prompted percutaneous biopsy of the mass and placement of a drain. Over the next several days, persistent sanguineous output from the drain led to anemia and concern for hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated an infrarenal IVC thrombus and a near-occlusive embolus in the left pulmonary artery. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed compression of the distal IVC at its junction with the right atrium, with otherwise normal biventricular function and no evidence of elevated right heart pressures.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver

candidate_registry.label: Inferior Vena Cava Thrombosis due to Tumor Invasion

A woman in her 50s presented with 4 days of blurry vision and pain in her left eye after undergoing a routine dental cleaning 1 week prior. She had no history of gingival disease or cavities. Her medical and ocular histories were unremarkable.

Visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/50 OS. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Left eye examination showed conjunctival hyperemia, faint keratic precipitates, 3+ cells with fibrin in the anterior chamber, mild nuclear sclerosis, and a whitish focal granuloma at the 4-o'clock position at the pupillary margin. The posterior segment was unremarkable, with no evidence of vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis. The right eye was unremarkable. At 1-day follow-up, visual acuity declined to 20/100 OS, with development of hypopyon and increased fibrinous material emanating from the iris lesion. No posterior segment involvement was noted.

- Microscopy: Gram stain revealed gram-positive cocci in chains and gram-positive rods in a branching pattern.  Image Title: Gram Stain of Iris Abscess  Image Description: Mixed flora of gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains and gram-positive bacilli (original magnification ×400)- Cultures: Aerobic culture revealed Streptococcus intermedius. The gram-positive bacilli could not be identified more specifically.- Additional Tests: Blood and urine cultures, electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were unremarkable.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
